sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Stereotactic Radiosurgery (SRS) for Brain Tumours
sectionToMerge.intro: Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is a precise, non-surgical form of radiation therapy used for many brain tumours. These FAQs explain how it works, who may be eligible, what it costs, and how international patients can access treatment.

items.q: What is stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for brain tumours?
items.a: Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is a highly precise form of radiation therapy that delivers a strong, focused dose to a brain tumour in one or a few sessions, without any surgical incision. Despite its name, no cutting is involved. Instead, many finely targeted radiation beams converge on the tumour while sparing nearby healthy brain tissue. It is used for selected brain tumours and is planned by a specialist radiation oncology team.

items.q: How does SRS work to treat a brain tumour?
items.a: SRS works by aiming multiple radiation beams from different angles so they meet precisely at the tumour. Each individual beam is weak, but together they deliver a high, tumour-damaging dose at the target while surrounding brain tissue receives much less. Detailed imaging such as MRI and CT guides the plan. The radiation damages tumour-cell DNA, causing cells to stop growing or die gradually over weeks to months.

items.q: What machines are used to deliver SRS?
items.a: SRS is commonly delivered using systems such as Gamma Knife, CyberKnife, or a linear accelerator (LINAC) adapted for radiosurgery. Gamma Knife uses many cobalt sources focused on the brain, while CyberKnife and LINAC systems use robotic or gantry-based beams. Each has strengths depending on tumour size, location, and number. The choice depends on the equipment available and the recommendation of the treating radiation oncology team.

items.q: What types of brain tumours can be treated with SRS?
items.a: SRS may be used for several brain conditions, including brain metastases, acoustic neuromas, meningiomas, pituitary tumours, and some arteriovenous malformations. It is often considered for small, well-defined tumours or those in areas that are difficult to reach surgically. Larger tumours may need surgery, fractionated radiation, or a combination of treatments. Suitability depends on tumour type, size, location, number, and specialist review of the patient's imaging.

items.q: Who is eligible for SRS for brain tumours?
items.a: SRS may be suitable for selected patients with small to moderately sized brain tumours that are clearly defined on imaging. Eligibility depends on tumour type, size, number, location, previous treatment, and overall health. Patients with very large tumours or significant swelling may need surgery or other radiation approaches first. The final decision is made by a qualified radiation oncology and neurosurgery team after reviewing scans and medical history.

items.q: How should I prepare for SRS treatment?
items.a: Preparation for SRS usually begins with detailed imaging, such as high-resolution MRI and CT, to map the tumour precisely. Depending on the system used, a lightweight head frame or a custom moulded mask may be fitted to keep the head still. Your team may review current medications and advise on steroids to reduce swelling. Specific instructions on eating, medication, and arrival time are given by the treating centre.

items.q: How long does an SRS session take and is it painful?
items.a: An SRS session is painless and typically takes from about 30 minutes to a few hours, depending on the tumour and the system used. You remain awake and lie still while the machine delivers the radiation; you feel nothing during the beams. Frame placement, if used, may cause mild pressure. Most treatments are completed in a single day, though some plans use up to five sessions.

items.q: What are the side effects and risks of SRS?
items.a: SRS is generally well tolerated, but side effects can occur and vary between patients. Short-term effects may include tiredness, headache, mild nausea, or temporary swelling around the treated area. Less commonly, delayed effects such as radiation-related changes in brain tissue can develop months later. Risks depend on tumour size, location, and dose. Your radiation oncology team will explain the specific risks and monitor you with follow-up scans.

items.q: How effective is SRS and how soon are results seen?
items.a: SRS can effectively control the growth of many selected brain tumours, though results depend on tumour type, size, and biology. Tumours often shrink slowly or stop growing over weeks to months rather than disappearing immediately, so follow-up MRI scans are used to track the response. Outcomes vary between patients, and no radiation treatment can guarantee tumour control. Your specialist team will discuss realistic expectations for your situation.

items.q: How much does SRS for brain tumours cost?
items.a: The cost of SRS varies widely depending on the country, hospital, machine used, tumour complexity, and number of sessions. It is often more affordable in countries such as India compared with Western nations, but exact pricing cannot be fixed in advance. Final cost also depends on imaging, planning, hospital stay, and additional treatment. A personalised estimate should be obtained from the chosen hospital after medical record review.

Many of these centres treat both domestic and international patients. Availability of a specific technology varies by hospital and city. The most appropriate centre depends on the tumour type and the recommendation of the treating radiation oncology and neurosurgery team.

items.q: Which countries offer SRS for brain tumours?
items.a: SRS is offered in many countries, including India, the United States, Germany, Turkey, Singapore, and others with advanced radiation oncology facilities. Availability of specific systems such as Gamma Knife or CyberKnife differs between hospitals and regions. Patients often choose a centre based on cost, expertise, technology, and travel convenience. The right destination should be decided together with medical advisors and the treating team after reviewing the diagnosis.

Coverage for SRS depends on your insurance provider, policy terms, country, and the reason for treatment. Some insurers cover radiosurgery when it is medically indicated, while others may require pre-authorisation or apply limits. International patients often pay directly and may later claim reimbursement, depending on their policy. It is best to confirm coverage, documentation, and approval requirements with your insurer and the hospital before treatment begins.

items.q: How does SRS compare with traditional brain surgery?
items.a: SRS differs from traditional brain surgery in that it uses focused radiation instead of an incision, so there is no cutting, general anaesthesia, or long hospital stay in most cases. Surgery may be preferred for large tumours, tumours causing pressure, or when tissue is needed for diagnosis. SRS may suit small or hard-to-reach tumours. The best approach depends on the tumour and specialist assessment of each patient.

items.q: Can SRS be combined with other cancer treatments?
items.a: Yes, SRS may be combined with other treatments depending on the tumour type and overall plan. For example, it may be used after surgery to treat remaining tumour, alongside whole-brain radiation in selected cases, or together with systemic therapies such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy. The combination and timing depend on cancer type, biomarkers, and previous treatment, and should be decided by a multidisciplinary oncology team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for SRS in brain tumours?
items.a: Clinical trials studying SRS for brain tumours are ongoing in several countries, often exploring new dosing, combinations with drug therapies, or treatment of specific tumour types. Participation may offer access to newer approaches but cannot guarantee benefit. Eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment, and trials usually have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Your oncology team can advise whether a relevant trial may be appropriate.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan SRS abroad?
items.a: To plan SRS abroad, hospitals usually need recent brain imaging such as MRI and CT scans, pathology or biopsy reports if available, and a summary of your diagnosis and previous treatment. Details of current medications and other health conditions are also helpful. These records allow the radiation oncology team to assess suitability and provide an estimate. A second opinion may be recommended before finalising any treatment decision.

items.q: How can international patients access SRS treatment?
items.a: International patients can access SRS by sharing their medical reports with a suitable hospital, obtaining a treatment plan and estimate, and then arranging travel and admission. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, and fitness to travel, none of which can be guaranteed in advance. Planning should also consider length of stay, caregiver support, and follow-up care after returning home, ideally coordinated with local doctors.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with SRS for brain tumours?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, tumour type, imaging, previous treatment, and overall health. CancerFax provides guidance and coordination but does not replace the medical judgement of the treating doctors and hospital.
